focus: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs

items.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
items.why: HNSW is the default index inside most vector databases and RAG stacks (pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Lucene/OpenSearch). Knowing the algorithm lets you reason about recall vs latency vs memory instead of cargo-culting M and ef values, and it is the natural bridge between data-structure theory (skip lists, Delaunay graphs) and production retrieval quality.
items.summary:
The index is a stack of proximity graphs over nested subsets of the data. Every element draws a max layer l = floor(-ln(U) * mL), so layer membership decays exponentially (with mL = 1/ln(M), P(level >= k) = M^-k). Layer 0 holds everything; one global entry point lives at the top layer. This is essentially a skip list where the express lanes are neighbor graphs rather than linked lists.

Insertion first greedy-descends from the top layer to layer l+1 using a search with ef=1, carrying the closest node down as the entry point. From min(L,l) down to layer 0 it runs a beam search with efConstruction candidates, picks M neighbors, links bidirectionally, and re-prunes any neighbor whose degree exceeds Mmax (Mmax0 on layer 0; the paper suggests about 2*M there). If l exceeds the current top layer, the new node becomes the entry point.

Search-layer keeps a candidate min-queue and a bounded result set of size ef. It pops the closest candidate and stops when that candidate is farther than the worst element of the result set, otherwise expanding its unvisited neighbors. A query is greedy descent through the upper layers, then this beam search on layer 0, returning the K nearest from the ef set. ef is the query-time recall knob.

The subtle part is neighbor selection. The simple rule takes the M closest candidates. The heuristic walks candidates nearest-first and keeps one only if it is closer to the base point than to every neighbor already selected, which approximates a relative-neighborhood-graph pruning. This preserves long-range links between clusters and keeps the graph navigable on clustered data; the paper reports it matches or beats the simple rule in all tested cases. Optionally pruned candidates can be used to fill remaining slots.

Complexity: under a Delaunay-graph idealization, expected steps per layer are constant and layers are O(log N), giving logarithmic search; construction is O(N log N) in low dimension. The authors are candid that this argument weakens in high dimensions. M controls memory and the recall ceiling (the paper suggests 5 to 48 as a reasonable range), and efConstruction trades build time for graph quality.
items.exercise: Implement HNSW in about 200 lines of Python or C# (layer assignment, SEARCH-LAYER with two heaps, heuristic neighbor selection). Index 50k SIFT or random 128-d vectors, then sweep ef in {10,20,50,100,200} and plot recall@10 against queries per second versus brute force. Then swap the heuristic selection for the simple M-closest rule on a clustered synthetic dataset and measure the recall drop.

items.title: Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg
items.source: Verma, Pedrosa, Korupolu, Oppenheimer, Tune, Wilkes; EuroSys 2015 (Google Research)
items.why: Borg is the direct ancestor of Kubernetes, and its scheduler design explains many behaviors you hit on AKS and GKE: priority and preemption, quota vs scheduling, why kube-scheduler caches and scores. It is also a masterclass in the cost-model reasoning (utilization, cell compaction) behind cloud capacity decisions.
items.summary:
Each cell has a logically centralized Borgmaster (five replicas, one Paxos-elected leader holding in-memory state with snapshot plus change-log checkpoints) and a Borglet agent on every machine. The master polls Borglets, with stateless link shards forwarding only diffs; Borglets keep running tasks if they lose the master. Scheduling is a separate process working on a cached copy of cell state, with assignments accepted unless stale, which is optimistic concurrency in the spirit of Omega.

Workloads are jobs of tasks (Linux processes in containers, not VMs) with per-dimension resource requests rather than fixed slots, plus allocs, reserved resource envelopes that several tasks can share (the precursor of the pod-with-sidecars pattern). Priority bands run monitoring, production, batch, best-effort; production tasks cannot preempt each other, which prevents preemption cascades. Quota is enforced at admission, not at scheduling time, and lower-priority quota is oversold.

The scheduler scans pending work from high to low priority. It runs feasibility checking (constraints plus enough available resources, counting evictable lower-priority tasks as available), then scoring with a hybrid model aimed at minimizing stranded resources, which the paper reports packs a few percent better than best fit. Three tricks make this scale: score caching, equivalence classes (evaluate once per group of identical tasks), and relaxed randomization (examine machines in random order until enough feasible ones are found). Without them a full reschedule did not finish in days; with them it took a few hundred seconds.

The utilization findings are the most transferable. Using cell compaction (re-pack the workload from scratch to find the smallest cell that fits), segregating prod from non-prod would need roughly 20 to 30 percent more machines in the median cell, and giving each user a private cell would need far more. Sharing is what pays for the fleet. Availability comes from declarative desired state, idempotent operations, spreading across failure domains, and rate-limiting rescheduling when a machine failure cannot be told apart from a network partition. Note: the later sections on isolation and lessons were only partially verified when preparing this digest.
items.exercise: Write a small scheduler simulator in Python: generate 5k machines and 50k tasks with CPU/RAM requests, implement feasibility plus scoring with (a) best fit, (b) worst fit, (c) a hybrid, and add relaxed randomization (stop after examining k feasible machines). Measure stranded resources and scheduling time per task for each strategy, then add equivalence-class caching and report the speedup.

items.title: A Detailed Look at RFC 8446 (a.k.a. TLS 1.3)
items.why: TLS terminates nearly every service you run, including healthcare traffic under HIPAA-style requirements. Understanding what TLS 1.3 removed and why (RSA key exchange, CBC, MAC-then-encrypt) gives you a security mental model rooted in real attacks, and the 0-RTT replay caveat is a classic distributed-systems idempotency problem in disguise.
items.summary:
TLS 1.2 needs two round trips before application data on a fresh connection. TLS 1.3 cuts a full handshake to one by having the client send key shares speculatively in its first flight; if the server wants a different group it answers with a HelloRetryRequest, which should be rare.

The protocol was pruned hard. Static RSA key exchange is gone (no forward secrecy, exposed to Bleichenbacher-style padding oracles), so only ephemeral Diffie-Hellman remains, restricted to a small set of named groups such as X25519 and P-256 instead of peer-chosen parameters that some implementations got badly wrong. CBC and stream ciphers like RC4 are gone, MAC-then-encrypt is gone (the root of BEAST and Lucky 13 style attacks), and only AEAD ciphers remain. PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures give way to RSA-PSS. The old monolithic cipher suites become three independent negotiations: cipher plus HKDF hash, key exchange group, and signature algorithm.

Downgrade resistance improves because the server signs the whole handshake transcript, including the negotiation, which addresses the FREAK, Logjam and similar class of attacks where an attacker forced weak export-grade parameters. Session resumption uses a PSK derived from a prior session and carried by a session ticket.

0-RTT lets a resuming client send application data in its first flight, saving a round trip, but that data is replayable: the server has not contributed any freshness before accepting it. Mitigations are to restrict 0-RTT to safe idempotent requests and to have servers reject early data when ticket age looks off. Note: the key-schedule derivation is not covered in detail by this post; read RFC 8446 section 7 alongside it.
items.exercise: Using Python's cryptography library, implement the HKDF-Extract/Expand key schedule from RFC 8446 section 7.1 for a PSK-less handshake (early secret, handshake secret, master secret, HKDF-Expand-Label with the 'tls13 ' prefix). Validate it against the test vectors in RFC 8448, then capture a real handshake with openssl s_client -tls1_3 and Wireshark and identify each message in the 1-RTT flow.

items.title: Rust Atomics and Locks, Chapter 3: Memory Ordering
items.why: Lock-free code is where compilers, CPUs and the language memory model all interact, and the C++/Rust model here is the same one underlying .NET's Volatile and Interlocked reasoning, Java's VarHandles and Go's sync/atomic. This chapter is the cleanest treatment of happens-before and acquire/release available, and it directly sharpens how you review concurrent code.
items.summary:
The starting point is that compilers and processors freely reorder or rewrite code as long as single-threaded behavior is preserved, for example fusing two increments of one variable across an unrelated store. That reasoning ignores other threads, so atomics need explicit orderings. Rust's model is the abstract C++ model, not any one CPU, and Rust omits C++ consume ordering because no compiler implements it faithfully.

The organizing concept is happens-before. Within a thread it is program order; across threads it arises from spawn and join, mutex unlock and lock, and non-Relaxed atomic operations. Relaxed operations guarantee only a single total modification order per variable, so every thread sees the same sequence of values for that one atomic, but give no ordering relative to other variables. The chapter's example shows a reader legitimately observing Y=20 while still reading X=0 even though the writer stored X first.

Release/Acquire is the workhorse. A release store that is observed by an acquire load creates a happens-before edge, making everything the writer did earlier visible to the reader afterward. The canonical example stores DATA relaxed, then READY with release; a reader spinning on READY with acquire is guaranteed to see the data. The chapter builds a spinlock (acquire on lock, release on unlock) and lazy initialization via compare_exchange on an AtomicPtr, and explains that synchronization chains through read-modify-write operations but is broken by a plain store.

SeqCst adds a single global order across all SeqCst operations and is mainly needed for store-then-load patterns such as flag-based mutual exclusion; it is not a safe default and cannot conjure a release-load or acquire-store. Fences decouple ordering from the operation and can cover several variables or apply conditionally; a release fence plus relaxed store is equivalent to a release store. The chapter closes with misconceptions, notably that Relaxed does not mean delayed and that disabling compiler optimizations does not stop hardware reordering. Note: the later fences and misconceptions parts were only partially verified when preparing this digest.
items.exercise: Implement a bounded SPSC ring buffer in Rust (or C# with Volatile.Read/Write and Interlocked) using acquire/release on the head and tail indices. Stress test it with a producer pushing a monotonically increasing counter and a consumer checking order, then deliberately downgrade the orderings to Relaxed and run under loom (Rust) or on an ARM machine to see whether you can provoke a violation. Benchmark against a mutex-protected queue.
